abstract.t: This document defines an optional, non-transitive BGP path attribute, NEXT_HOP_MTU, whose type code is TBD. The attribute carries the IP MTU available for a BGP NLRI across a network boundary. The BGP speaker that receives the NLRI may add the attribute from the IP MTU of that boundary. The value is a promissory commitment that an IP packet of the indicated size is acceptable across the boundary. Applications on internal BGP sessions and on external BGP sessions can use the value.

note.name: Discussion Venues
note.t: This document is an individual submission intended for consideration by the Inter-Domain Routing (IDR) Working Group. Discussion takes place on the IDR mailing list (idr@ietf.org), which is archived at .

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Networks often accept IP packets larger than the conventional 1500-octet Ethernet payload at a network boundary. A common case is an interface configured so that an IP packet of 9000 octets can cross the boundary. Hosts, tunnel endpoints, and other routers inside a network can use that size when they know it. They learn reachability through BGP, but BGP itself has no way to carry the IP MTU of the boundary with the route.

This document defines the NEXT_HOP_MTU path attribute. The attribute is optional. Its type code is assigned by IANA and is TBD in this version of the document. It is associated with the NLRI carried in the same BGP UPDATE message. The value is the IP MTU, in octets, that the attaching speaker promises is acceptable for traffic toward those NLRI across one network boundary.

The speaker that receives a route across the boundary is the speaker that adds the attribute. It uses the IP MTU of its interface on that boundary. It can then make the value available to internal peers and, when it advertises the route onward, to external peers. The attribute describes that boundary. It is a single promissory value for the NLRI at that boundary. A speaker replaces the value only when computes a new value for a different boundary.

Path MTU Discovery and Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery remain the mechanisms that find the minimum MTU of a whole path (, , ). BGP-LS can distribute the MTU of individual links in a link-state topology (, ). NEXT_HOP_MTU gives a BGP speaker a promissory IP MTU for an ordinary unicast NLRI at the network boundary where the route was learned.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the BGP terminology of and .

dl.dd: The size, in octets, of the largest IP packet that can cross a link in one piece. The IP packet includes the IP header and the IP payload. Link-layer headers are excluded. This size is what the network boundary promises is acceptable. An interface that permits an IP payload of 9000 octets has an IP MTU of 9000 for this attribute.
The edge between two networks across which traffic toward an NLRI is forwarded. In the example in , the network boundary is the link between AS 65000 and AS 65001.
A value the attaching BGP speaker includes as its promise that an IP packet of that size, destined to the NLRI, is acceptable across the network boundary.
A BGP session between speakers in the same autonomous system (internal BGP).
A BGP session between speakers in different autonomous systems (external BGP).

section.name: NEXT_HOP_MTU Attribute
section.t: NEXT_HOP_MTU is an optional, non-transitive BGP path attribute. The attribute type code is TBD, to be assigned by IANA from the BGP Path Attributes registry ().

The attribute applies to every NLRI in the UPDATE message that carries it. Those NLRI are the destinations for which the promissory value holds. IPv4 unicast NLRI use the encoding in . IPv6 unicast NLRI, and IPv4 unicast NLRI carried as multiprotocol NLRI, use MP_REACH_NLRI as specified in . NEXT_HOP_MTU is a path attribute alongside MP_REACH_NLRI. It is not encoded inside the NLRI.

This attribute is defined for IPv4 unicast (AFI 1, SAFI 1) and IPv6 unicast (AFI 2, SAFI 1). A speaker MUST NOT attach NEXT_HOP_MTU to an UPDATE for any other AFI or SAFI. Use with other address families is outside the scope of this document.

section.name: Attribute Header
section.t: The attribute header is the three-octet path-attribute header defined in : one octet of flags, one octet of type code, and one octet of length. The value field follows the header and is four octets long, so the Extended Length bit is clear and the one-octet length is sufficient.

The flags octet MUST be 0x80 when a speaker attaches the attribute: the Optional bit is 1, and the Transitive, Partial, Extended Length, and reserved bits are 0. restates those bits. Bit 0 is the high-order bit.
The type code is TBD (one octet). The length is 4. A speaker that does not recognize the type code follows the optional non-transitive rules in : it ignores the attribute and does not propagate it.

section.name: IP MTU Value
section.t: The IP MTU field is an unsigned 32-bit integer in network byte order. It is the maximum IP packet size, in octets, that the attaching speaker promises is acceptable across the network boundary for the NLRI in the UPDATE. The size includes the IP header and the IP payload and excludes link-layer framing.

For IPv4 NLRI the value MUST be greater than or equal to 68 and less than or equal to 65535. 68 octets is the smallest IP datagram every internet module must be able to forward without further fragmentation (). 65535 octets is the largest value that fits in the IPv4 Total Length field. For IPv6 NLRI the value MUST be greater than or equal to 1280 and less than or equal to 4294967295. 1280 octets is the minimum IPv6 link MTU (). Values greater than 65535 are used for IPv6 jumbograms ().
A value of 9000 means that an IP packet of 9000 octets is acceptable.

section.name: Network Boundary
section.t: The network boundary of a received route is the interface on which the receiving speaker forwards traffic toward the BGP next hop of that route, when that interface is the edge the route was learned across. For a directly connected external session, this is the interface of the session. The IP MTU of the boundary is the IP MTU of that interface for the address family of the NLRI.

An internal interface is not a network boundary for a route that was learned across a different edge. A speaker MUST NOT replace NEXT_HOP_MTU with the IP MTU of an internal interface when it readvertises such a route.

If the BGP next hop is not reached through the interface the session was received on, as with a multi-hop external session, the speaker MUST NOT invent a boundary from an unrelated interface. The speaker MAY attach the attribute when the operator has configured a promissory value for that neighbor. A configured value MUST be less than or equal to the IP MTU of the interface that actually forwards traffic toward the next hop.

section.name: Adding the Attribute on Receipt
section.t: The BGP speaker that receives an NLRI across a network boundary MAY add NEXT_HOP_MTU to that route. The speaker adds the attribute when it installs the route for local use and when it advertises the route. The route does not need to have arrived with the attribute already present. shows this case. The receiving router adds the attribute from the boundary interface.
The speaker computes the attached value as follows.

ol.li: Let L be the IP MTU, in octets, of the network boundary. If L cannot be determined, the speaker MUST NOT attach the attribute.
If the NLRI are IPv4 and L is less than 68 or greater than 65535, or the NLRI are IPv6 and L is less than 1280 or greater than 4294967295, the speaker MUST NOT attach the attribute.
If the received route contains a valid NEXT_HOP_MTU value R and local policy accepts R from that neighbor, the attached value is the minimum of L and R. Otherwise the attached value is L.
Local policy MAY reduce the attached value further. Policy MUST NOT increase it. The result MUST still satisfy the range for the address family in .

section.t: All NLRI in one UPDATE MUST share one NEXT_HOP_MTU value when the attribute is present. A speaker MAY place several NLRI that share a value into one UPDATE. NLRI that do not share a value MUST be advertised in separate UPDATE messages.
Absence of the attribute means the speaker makes no promise. Consumers MUST treat absence as lack of information. Absence does not imply 1500, 1280, 68, or any other default.

section.name: Internal and External Sessions
section.t: NEXT_HOP_MTU MAY be carried on internal sessions and on external sessions. Internal applications include internal peers, route reflectors, and functions on the receiving speaker that choose a packet size for the NLRI. External applications include the external peer that receives the attribute, and functions in that neighboring network that use the promissory value for traffic toward the NLRI.

An implementation MUST provide configuration to enable or disable attachment of the attribute, and configuration to enable or disable acceptance of a received value, per neighbor and per AFI and SAFI. This document does not require either behavior to be enabled on a session by default. The example in assumes the receiving speaker is configured to add the attribute.

On an internal session, a speaker that does not itself forward traffic across a different network boundary for the NLRI SHOULD advertise the attribute unchanged when the route already has one and the BGP next hop is unchanged. A route reflector that does not change the next hop SHOULD forward the attribute unchanged ().

The border speaker that learned the route across the network boundary SHOULD include the value it computed in when it advertises the route to internal peers. That remains true when the border speaker replaces the BGP next hop with its own address. Traffic from internal peers still crosses the same network boundary, so the promissory value is still the IP MTU of that boundary.

On an external session, the value a speaker attaches MUST be the promissory value for traffic that crosses the boundary with that peer toward the NLRI. When the route already carries a valid NEXT_HOP_MTU and the speaker also knows the IP MTU of the interface facing that peer, the attached value MUST be the minimum of those two numbers, then reduced by local policy if policy reduces it. The speaker MUST NOT copy a promise about one boundary onto a session that crosses a different boundary without applying that minimum. If the speaker cannot determine the value for the session it is advertising on, it MUST omit the attribute.

A speaker that originates an NLRI MAY attach NEXT_HOP_MTU when it advertises the route. The value is the IP MTU of the network boundary the advertisement is sent across, subject to the minimums in . Origination is optional. The receiving speaker can add the attribute from its own side of the boundary whether or not the originator sent one.

section.name: Promissory Semantics
section.t: By attaching NEXT_HOP_MTU, a speaker promises that an IP packet destined to a covered NLRI, of size less than or equal to the attribute value, is acceptable across the network boundary. Acceptable means the boundary interface permits a packet of that size and the attaching speaker will forward such a packet across that boundary toward the NLRI.

The promise covers that boundary. An application MAY use the value as the IP packet size it sends toward the NLRI when the packet will cross the boundary identified by the route. An application that needs the minimum MTU of every link between a source and a destination continues to use Path MTU Discovery (, ) or Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery ().
NEXT_HOP_MTU MUST NOT by itself change the result of the BGP Decision Process (). Local policy MAY select or prefer a route using the attribute. Policy that does so is a local matter.

section.name: Forwarding and Multiple Paths
section.t: A speaker MAY program the promissory value as a per-destination forwarding MTU for the NLRI. It MAY do so only when every path it uses to forward traffic to that NLRI carries a valid NEXT_HOP_MTU. The programmed value MUST be the minimum of the values on those paths. If any path used for forwarding has no attribute, the speaker MUST NOT program a promissory MTU for the combined destination.
Each path has its own path attributes. Two paths for the same NLRI may carry different NEXT_HOP_MTU values when they were learned across different boundaries.

section.name: Aggregation
section.t: When a speaker aggregates component routes into a less specific NLRI, it MAY attach NEXT_HOP_MTU to the aggregate only when every component route included in the aggregate has a valid NEXT_HOP_MTU. The value MUST be the minimum of the component values. If any included component has no attribute, the speaker MUST omit NEXT_HOP_MTU from the aggregate.

section.name: Changes of Interface MTU
section.t: When the IP MTU of a network boundary changes, the speaker that attached NEXT_HOP_MTU from that boundary MUST advertise a replacement route for each affected NLRI. The replacement carries the new value computed by . If the speaker no longer makes a promise, the replacement omits the attribute. BGP has no withdraw for a single path attribute. Replacement of the route is the update.

section.name: Example
section.t: shows AS 65000 and AS 65001 exchanging the documentation prefix 2001:db8::/48 (). AS 65000 and AS 65001 are private AS numbers (). Router A in AS 65000 advertises the prefix to Router B in AS 65001. The boundary interface permits an IP payload of 9000 octets. Router B, the receiving router, adds NEXT_HOP_MTU with the value 9000 and advertises the route to Router C inside AS 65001.
The boundary subnet 2001:db8:1::/64 is outside the advertised prefix 2001:db8::/48. Router A's address on the boundary is 2001:db8:1::1. Router B's address on the boundary is 2001:db8:1::2.

ol.li: Router A advertises 2001:db8::/48 to Router B. The advertisement need not include NEXT_HOP_MTU. Router A MAY include it, with the value 9000, as its own promise for the same boundary.
The interface on Router B toward Router A has an IP MTU that permits an IP payload of 9000 octets. That interface is the network boundary for this NLRI.

Router B receives the NLRI and adds NEXT_HOP_MTU with the value 9000. If Router A also sent the value 9000 and Router B accepts it, the minimum is still 9000. If Router A had sent a smaller valid value, Router B would attach that smaller value.

Router B advertises the route to Router C on an internal session, including NEXT_HOP_MTU 9000. Router C is an internal application of the promissory value. Router C can treat an IP packet of 9000 octets as acceptable when that packet will cross this boundary toward 2001:db8::/48.
The same procedure applies to a prefix AS 65001 advertises to AS 65000. The router that receives the prefix adds the attribute from the IP MTU of its own boundary interface.

Traffic toward 2001:db8::/48 flows from Router C to Router B and then across the boundary to Router A. The promissory value 9000 applies to IP packets on that crossing. An external application uses the same attribute when a speaker includes it on an external advertisement. The value on that advertisement is computed for the boundary that traffic from that external peer will cross, as specified in .

section.name: Error Handling
section.t: NEXT_HOP_MTU errors use the attribute discard approach of . The malformed attribute is discarded and the UPDATE is processed as if the attribute had not been present. The speaker MUST NOT use a discarded value as a promissory MTU. These errors MUST NOT cause a BGP NOTIFICATION and MUST NOT cause the NLRI to be treated as withdrawn. A malformed optional hint is discarded so that it cannot remove reachability.
A speaker MUST discard the attribute as malformed when any of the following is true:

ul.li: The attribute appears more than once in the UPDATE.
The Optional bit is 0, the Transitive bit is 1, the Partial bit is 1, the Extended Length bit is 1, or any reserved flag bit is 1.
The UPDATE carries IPv4 unicast NLRI and the value is less than 68 or greater than 65535.
The UPDATE carries IPv6 unicast NLRI and the value is less than 1280.
The UPDATE carries NLRI for an AFI or SAFI other than IPv4 unicast or IPv6 unicast.

section.t: A value that meets the checks above is syntactically valid. Whether the neighbor is permitted to constrain the local promise with that value is a matter of policy ().

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: Operators who want a receiving router to publish a boundary MTU enable attachment on that router for the neighbors that should receive the promise. In , Router B is enabled to add NEXT_HOP_MTU for the internal session toward Router C. Router B's boundary interface is configured with an IP MTU of 9000 before the attribute can promise 9000.

Both ends of a boundary are normally configured with the same IP MTU. The receiving speaker promises the size its own interface permits. When the advertising peer also sends NEXT_HOP_MTU and the receiver accepts it, the value propagated inside the receiving AS is the minimum of the two, which covers the case where the two ends differ.

Internal consumers can use the value as a per-destination forwarding MTU, as a packetization limit for traffic they originate toward the NLRI, or as input to an encapsulation function that subtracts its own overhead from the promissory size. External consumers can use a value received on an external session in the same ways, for traffic that will cross the boundary the advertisement described.
TCP MSS clamping and Path MTU Discovery continue to apply. NEXT_HOP_MTU does not remove the need for them on paths that extend past the boundary identified by the route.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: NEXT_HOP_MTU is a promise that another speaker may use to choose an IP packet size. A value larger than the size the boundary will actually accept can cause packet loss when senders transmit packets the boundary drops. A value smaller than the size the boundary will accept causes senders to use smaller packets. That reduces efficiency and can interact with tunnel overhead and with Path MTU Discovery.

The speaker that adds the attribute on receipt derives the value from its own interface MTU. That local measurement limits exposure to a peer that overstates its MTU. When a received value is accepted, it can only reduce the attached value, because the attached value is the minimum of the local boundary IP MTU and the received value. A peer can still offer a smaller value and cause this speaker to propagate that smaller promise. Acceptance of a received value is therefore a configuration choice per neighbor (). Operators SHOULD enable acceptance from an external peer only when that peer is trusted to state a boundary MTU.
Advertising the attribute tells the receiving peer the IP MTU of a network boundary. Operators who treat that MTU as sensitive can disable attachment toward the peers in question.

This document defines no new session authentication. The existing protection of the BGP session applies. Operational guidance for protecting BGP sessions is discussed in . Malformed NEXT_HOP_MTU attributes are discarded without a session reset and without withdrawing the NLRI (), so a corrupt or hostile optional value cannot be used to drop the session or to remove the route.
